entities.name: Timurid dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Timurid Empire (1370–1507) was a Turco-Mongol empire founded by Timur (Tamerlane) in Central Asia, with Samarkand as its magnificent capital. One of history's most feared conquerors, Timur's campaigns from Anatolia to Delhi left millions dead and cities in ruin, yet his Timurid successors presided over one of the Islamic world's greatest cultural renaissances in Samarkand, Bukhara, and Herat.

Timur's military campaigns between 1370 and 1405 CE crushed the Ottoman Turks at Ankara (1402), sacked Delhi (1398) killing 100,000, and devastated the Golden Horde. He built towers of skulls from conquered enemies as a psychological weapon and killed an estimated 17 million people — 5% of the world's population at that time. Samarkand, beautified with the spoils of conquest, featured the Registan mosque complex and the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum (Timur's own tomb), still standing as masterworks of Islamic architecture.

The Timurid cultural renaissance under Timur's successors — particularly Shahrukh, Ulugh Beg, and Sultan Husayn Bayqara — produced extraordinary achievements: Ulugh Beg built the world's most advanced pre-telescopic observatory, his astronomical tables remaining accurate for centuries. Persian miniature painting reached its classical peak. The poet Jami, the philosopher Mir Ali Shir Nava'i, and Herat's literary circle set standards that influenced Mughal India and Safavid Persia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Timurid Empire combined history's most destructive conqueror with a cultural golden age that transmitted Islamic-Persian aesthetics to Mughal India and Safavid Persia, shaping South and Central Asian civilization for centuries.
